submissions.findingTextShort: Traditional aqueous Kava cannot be treated as categorically free of liver-injury risk.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: PMID 12923378 reported two hepatitis cases in which traditional aqueous Kava root extracts were considered the most probable cause, plus a survey of 27 heavy Kava drinkers with frequent GGT elevation and only minimal transaminase elevation in a minority. The authors interpreted the isolated GGT pattern as likely CYP450 induction rather than liver injury. This supports a rare-event safety boundary for aqueous preparations while preventing isolated GGT elevation from being mislabeled as hepatitis.
submissions.populationContext: Two human hepatitis cases plus 27 heavy Kava drinkers in New Caledonia.
submissions.usageContext: Traditional aqueous Kava root preparations; exposure in heavy drinkers is not interchangeable with standardized medicinal tablets.
submissions.safetyContext: Aqueous preparation is not a zero-risk category, but the observational survey does not establish incidence or a toxic dose.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Case evidence cannot quantify population risk; isolated GGT elevation should not be equated with hepatocellular injury.

submissions.findingTextShort: Historical Kava-associated hepatitis case series included severe and fulminant outcomes, but does not provide an incidence estimate.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: PMID 12821045 analyzed 29 new hepatitis cases associated with Kava ingestion plus seven previously published reports. Both alcoholic and acetonic extracts were represented; nine patients developed fulminant liver failure, eight underwent transplantation, and three died. The case-series design supports severity awareness but cannot establish population incidence, universal causality, or a safe/toxic dose threshold.
submissions.populationContext: Thirty-six reported hepatitis cases considered in a clinical adverse-hepatic-reaction assessment.
submissions.usageContext: Predominantly medicinal alcoholic/acetonic Kava extracts; not automatically transferable to every Kava preparation.
submissions.safetyContext: Rare Kava-associated liver injury can be severe; case ascertainment cannot quantify absolute risk.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Spontaneous/case-series evidence is vulnerable to selection, co-exposure and causality uncertainty and must coexist with structured reassessments.

submissions.findingTextShort: Structured causality reassessment substantially downgraded many regulator-attributed Kava liver cases.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: PMID 20831679 reassessed 26 German/Swiss suspected Kava hepatotoxicity cases with two quantitative causality methods. The Maria-Victorino method classified most cases as unlikely or excluded; CIOMS classified only a minority as highly probable/probable/possible and excluded or downgraded many others. This is a first-class causality counterweight: reported case counts cannot be treated as equivalent to confirmed Kava-caused injuries.
submissions.populationContext: Twenty-six suspected hepatotoxicity cases previously considered by regulators.
submissions.usageContext: Causality-method analysis rather than an incidence or intervention study.
submissions.safetyContext: Preserves genuine safety concern while preventing inflation of suspected reports into confirmed causal events.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Different causality instruments produced different classifications; this does not prove Kava is liver-safe.

submissions.findingTextShort: Solvent choice alone cannot support a claim that aqueous Kava is hepatotoxicity-proof.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: PMID 19501269 used structured CIOMS assessment and reported established causality in cases involving aqueous Kava extracts or Kava-herb mixtures as well as cases involving ethanolic/acetonic extracts. The authors found similar clinical pictures across preparation classes. This directly blocks a simplistic solvent-only safety narrative, while leaving cultivar, plant-part, product-quality and co-exposure hypotheses unresolved.
submissions.populationContext: Case-based causality assessment across aqueous, ethanolic, acetonic and mixed Kava products.
submissions.usageContext: Preparation-comparison safety evidence; not an RCT and not a population-risk estimate.
submissions.safetyContext: Traditional/aqueous preparation may differ in risk but cannot be described as guaranteeing absence of hepatotoxicity.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Case-based causality and product heterogeneity limit mechanistic certainty; solvent independence does not identify a single toxic constituent.

submissions.findingTextShort: Flavokawain/APAP mouse findings are mechanistic interaction evidence, not a proven human acetaminophen interaction.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: PMID 25185080 found that flavokawains A and B potentiated acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity in C57BL/6 mice, whereas dihydromethysticin did not in the tested model. This supports a constituent-specific preclinical interaction hypothesis and product-composition concern, but it cannot be converted into a quantified human interaction, clinical contraindication, or proof that all Kava products behave identically.
submissions.populationContext: C57BL/6 mouse toxicology model; not human clinical evidence.
submissions.usageContext: Isolated/constituent-focused Kava toxicology with acetaminophen challenge.
submissions.safetyContext: Potential constituent-specific interaction mechanism; human magnitude and clinical relevance remain unestablished by this study.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Species, exposure and constituent composition prevent direct transfer to consumer products or human dosing.
